The ring flags Shiny app

Source: vignettes/flags-app.Rmd
flags-app.Rmd
library(rxs2tria)

Overview

Once cell and ring measurements have been compiled and cleaned (with complete_QWAdata(), see vignette("workflow")), it may be helpful to visually inspect the resulting measurement series. This allows you to check whether

  • the automatically estimated ring flags (wedging/missing rings, radially incomplete rings, overlapping/duplicate rings) are correct;
  • there are any gaps in the coverage, e.g. due to images that were forgotten in the analysis process;
  • there are other implausible values or outliers due to quality issues (e.g. decay, cracks, out-of-focus images) or discrete anatomical features (e.g. blue or frost rings, compression wood).

The ring flags app is an interactive quality-check tool: it plots the ring (or aggregated cell-level) measurement series for every woodpiece in your dataset, lets you click through individual years, and records data-quality and discrete-feature flags per ring in a table alongside the plot.

Note that this step is optional but we highly recommend using the app to ensure and improve the quality of your submission.

Launching the app 

launch_flags_app()

This requires a number of Suggested packages (bslib, collapse, htmlwidgets, plotly, reactable, rhandsontable, shiny, shinyjs, shinyvalidate), which rxs2tria will prompt you to install if missing.

(screenshot: app opened with no data loaded)

Providing input data

Click Load input data in the sidebar and choose a source (from the current R environment, or from CSV/JSON files) for up to three inputs:

  • QWA rings data (required): the $rings component of a QWAdata object, i.e. QWA_data$rings from Step 4 in the workflow.
  • Profile data (optional): a sector QWAprofile object (Step 6a of the workflow / see below) to allow also aggregated cell measurements as plotted QWA parameters in the time series.
  • ROXAS images metadata (optional): a QWAimages object, or the $images component of a QWAmetadata .json (Step 3b). This enables filtering by site/species, opening image files directly from the app (leveraging the values in the fname_image column), and the Comments tab described below.

(screenshot: input source modal)

Loading new data always overwrites what’s currently in the app, with a confirmation prompt if you have unsaved edits.

The QWAprofiles input

The optional Profile data input (a QWAprofile object) contains cell measurements aggregated across the ring width into n position bins of equal relative width (0–100% of ring width). To create such an object, run the following (cf. ?calculate_sector_profiles), before launching the flags app:

prf_sector <- calculate_sector_profiles(
  QWA_data, 
  n_sectors = 5,
  sel_cell_params = c("la", "cwttan"),
  quant_probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) 
# To save to file:
# write_QWAprofile(prf_sector, "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_QWAprofile_sector5.csv.gz")

The “Quality check series” tab

Filtering and plot settings

The sidebar lets you subset the data (by species, site, and/or woodpiece) and configure the main plot: which QWA parameter to show (ring-level, or an aggregated cell-level parameter from the profile data, with a sector selector), an optional 32-year spline detrend, the type of mean curve, and whether to show rings already marked for exclusion.

(screenshot: sidebar filters and plot settings)

The chronology plot

The main plot shows the measurement series for the selected woodpiece highlighted against all others in the current filter, with optional sample-depth and ring-coverage subplots underneath. Click any point to select that ring – clicking a point on a different woodpiece’s trace switches the selection to it. Once a ring is selected, use the arrow keys (or the arrow buttons above the ring table) to navigate to the previous/next ring (up/down arrows) or the previous/next image (left/right arrows). The enter/esc keys toggle the table focus. When the table is in focus, the left/right arrows navigate across the table columns instead.

(screenshot: chronology plot with a ring selected)

The ring flags table

Below the plot, a table shows every ring of the currently selected image, with editable columns for:

  • exclude_issues is the most important flag: it decides whether the ring should be excluded from analysis.
  • Four groups of checkboxes, customisable via the table’s gear icon: disqualifying issues (radially incomplete ring, wedging/missing ring, crossdating, compression wood, orientation), technical issues (out of focus, cracks, paraffin, compressed/overlapping/broken cells, tangentially incomplete, irregular thickness, air bubbles), other issues (tyloses, decay, other), and discrete features (blue/frost/ light ring, intra-annual density fluctuations, traumatic resin ducts, trabeculae, blue/red cells, other).
  • affected_tissue (all/ew/lw) to further specify which part of the ring is affected by the selected flags.
  • A free-text comment field.

In addition, there is the read-only column duplicate_ring, which indicates that the same year is also present in at least one other image. The corresponding exclude_dupl column defines for each group of overlapping years which one is the selected best. Specifically, for each distinct (woodpiece_label, year), exactly one image_label has exclude_dupl=FALSE, all others are set to TRUE. The default selected one is the ring with the highest cell count, but you can change this here. Editing exclude_dupl for one ring automatically applies the corresponding change to the other overlapping image(s).

Click Update excluded in plot to refresh the plot markers after editing exclusion flags.

(screenshot: ring flags table for a selected image)

If image metadata was loaded, you can also open the underlying image file directly (preferring an annotated version if one exists) via the image icon next to the selected image name.

The “Comments” tab

This tab only appears if the loaded image metadata included non-empty img_comment values (e.g. notes added during ROXAS AI processing, or manually in the metadata app’s Start tab table). It lists every commented image with a “handled” checkbox and a button to jump straight to that image/ring in the main tab, plus a badge showing how many comments are still unhandled – a convenient checklist to make sure every flagged image was actually looked at during the cleaning process.

(screenshot: comments overview table)

Saving your work

Click Save ring flags (or configure the destination first via the gear icon next to it) to write your edits to a local CSV file and/or an R environment variable. If a Comments tab was shown, its “handled” status is saved alongside it, to the images metadata file/variable, so you (or a colleague) can resume exactly where you left off.

(screenshot: save settings modal)

Exporting an rwl file

Click Export rwl to write the currently plotted parameter (and sector, for profile parameters) to a Tucson-format .rwl file, e.g. for crossdating or chronology building in other software. The export respects the current woodpiece filter and detrending setting, and removes duplicate and excluded rings based on the latest edits in the app (whether already updated in plot or not).

In the export dialog, you can adjust:

  • Scaling: the Tucson format stores values as integers with 5 digits (written at prec = 0.001). The suggested scaling converts ring widths (mrw, eww, lww, in μm) to mm. For other parameters, or detrended series, it picks the power of ten that makes the best use of the available digits. Untick the checkbox to enter a custom power of ten; values that would exceed the Tucson range are rejected. The scaling factor is included in the default file name, so the original values can be recovered by dividing by it.
  • File path for the .rwl file. Relative paths are resolved from the directory the app was launched in. If the rxsmeta data is loaded, series are named by short IDs derived from the data structure (e.g. YAM_LASI_122_a to YAM122a, see rename_for_tucson()). Otherwise, long labels are truncated by dplR::write.tucson(), which then saves a _mapping.txt file alongside the .rwl.

(screenshot: export rwl modal)

The same export can be scripted outside the app with extract_rwl(), rename_for_tucson(), scale_for_tucson() and dplR::write.tucson():

rwl <- extract_rwl(df_rings = QWA_data$rings, param = "mrw") |>
  rename_for_tucson(rxs_images, long.names = TRUE) |>
  scale_for_tucson(scaling = 0.001) # μm to mm
dplR::write.tucson(rwl, fname = "mrw.rwl", prec = 0.001, long.names = TRUE)

Output and how it fits into the workflow

The saved rings data is the $rings component of a QWAdata object, with the manually reviewed flag columns added or updated. Read it back and merge it into your QWAdata object to finish Step 6b of vignette("workflow"):

QWA_data$rings <- read_QWAdata(
  file_rings = "path/to/output_data/example_dataset_edited_QWArings.csv")$rings

write_QWAdata(QWA_data, dir = path_out, dataset_name = dataset_name)

If reviewing the data in the app reveals that one or more images need to be re-analysed in ROXAS/ROXAS AI, use update_QWAimages() and update_QWAdata() (Step 6c) to splice in the new results rather than reprocessing the whole dataset – by default this resets any manual flags for the updated images, since they may no longer apply to the re-analysed data.
